newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA SET TO DOUBLE PRESENCE IN SWAP MARKET.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA SET TO DOUBLE PRESENCE IN SWAP MARKET.

text.p: The Australian Treasury's plan to utilise domestic interest rate swaps to achieve funding and market risk management objectives should have little impact on the multi billion dollar market.

Tony Hinton, first assistant secretary of the Treasury's investment and debt division, indicated last week that the Australian government would require U.S. dollar exposure of around A$2.0 to 3.0 billion, allowing for scheduled maturities, to maintain its portfolio at its benchmark target.
Swap traders believe the market would not have any trouble in absorbing such a programme size.
"The reality is that A$2.0 to 3.0 billion in a year is really only scratching the surface," a senior trader said.
The Australian government is already a large player in the currency swap market, although its planned move into domestic swaps would effectively double its presence.
"The government is already the largest player in the swaps market, in that they have been swapping debt into U.S. dollar debt," Westpac chief economist Nigel Stapledon said.
"The Commonwealth had U.S. dollar exposure via the swaps market to the tune of A$3.0 billion last year and it will be the same this year," he said.
"Combine this activity with domestic swaps activity and the government is effectively doubling their presence in the swaps market," Stapledon said.
However, while the size of the programme would appear to have little impact, it will depend how the Treasury operates in the market.
Michael Berry, a trader with Colonial State Bank, said the government could make a significant difference if the planned swaps were done in a short space of time.
"If the government went in and hit the market with a large volume at a part of the yield curve where there was not a great appetite then there would be a problem," said Stapledon.
A senior swaps trader said that the swap market would be influenced if the government decided to do A$1.0 billion at the 10-year part of the curve.
"Otherwise, it's business as usual," he added.
